analysis.one_liner: Requires the Interior Department to hold a set number of oil and gas lease sales on public lands and offshore waters every year.
analysis.headline: A bill mandating dozens of annual oil and gas lease sales on federal land and offshore waters was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in February 2025 with 11 Republican cosponsors and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill tells the Interior Department exactly how many oil and gas lease sales it must hold each year: at least four in every state with federal land open to drilling, two a year in the Gulf of Mexico, and six over ten years in Alaska's Cook Inlet. It also bars any president from pausing or slowing federal energy leasing without Congress's approval. The bill extends and expands a ban on drilling in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida, which protects Florida's coasts from new offshore rigs.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: they would be guaranteed regular opportunities to lease public land and federal offshore waters on fixed terms, regardless of which administration is in office or what the market demands. Energy-producing states like Wyoming, Montana, New Mexico, and North Dakota gain a guaranteed stream of drilling activity and royalty revenue. Florida's coastal communities and tourism industry gain lasting protection from offshore drilling near their shores. Consumers could see marginal relief in energy supply over the long run.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers; energy-producing states

how_it_helps.text: Oil and gas companies get a guaranteed pipeline of federal leases: at least four onshore sales per year in each drilling-eligible state, two Gulf of Mexico sales per year through 2035, and six large Cook Inlet sales over a decade, with leases issued to the highest bidder within 90 days [S2][S3].

The bill strips the executive branch of the power to pause or slow federal energy leasing without congressional approval, so drilling access on public land and offshore waters would no longer depend on which party holds the White House [S2][S3].

The ban on drilling in the eastern Gulf of Mexico is extended through 2035 and expanded to the South Atlantic and Straits of Florida, protecting Florida and Atlantic coastal communities from new offshore rigs [S2][S3].
States with federal land open to drilling get guaranteed royalty-producing leasing activity, which supports jobs and state revenue in places like Wyoming, New Mexico, and Montana [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of having public land and ocean resources leased on whatever terms and schedule the bill fixes, with less room to weigh environmental review, market conditions, or conservation. Communities near expanded onshore drilling face the local effects of new wells. The Interior Department loses the flexibility to manage federal minerals in response to changing conditions; if a sale is canceled for any reason, including a lack of eligible parcels, it must hold a replacement sale the same year [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, federal land users, drilling-adjacent communities

drawbacks.text: The bill dictates lease sales "notwithstanding any other provision of law" and requires offering every parcel eligible under existing land-use plans, overriding the normal discretion federal agencies use to weigh wildlife, water, recreation, and climate impacts before leasing public land [S3].

If a lease sale is canceled, delayed, or deferred for any reason — even because there are no eligible parcels — the Secretary must hold a replacement sale the same year, forcing sales even when there is nothing appropriate to sell or little industry interest [S2][S3].
The Cook Inlet leases are locked at a 12.5% royalty rate, the standard minimum, giving taxpayers no share of any upside if the drilling proves unusually valuable [S3].

Mandating a fixed number of sales in every drilling-eligible state regardless of demand can produce leases that companies do not want, burdening agency budgets and producing paper sales rather than energy.
The constitutional balance it strikes is one-sided: a president could speed up leasing without congressional approval, but is barred from slowing it down [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main beneficiaries are oil and gas companies, which get guaranteed access to public land and offshore waters on fixed terms with political protection against any future administration that might slow leasing. The public gains are indirect and uncertain — more domestic drilling activity, revenue for energy-producing states, and real protection for Florida's coasts — while the costs are concrete: public resources leased on inflexible terms, weakened environmental review, and a one-way ratchet where drilling can only speed up, never slow down. The coastal drilling ban is the one provision with clear, direct value to ordinary people, and it is partly a concession that makes the rest of the bill easier to accept.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has not taken it up, and there is no sign of movement yet.

narrative.text: Senator Steve Daines introduced the bill on February 6, 2025, joined by 11 other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since [S5].
All 12 supporters are Republicans; no Democrat has cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet — the bill has gone nowhere, so the status quo holds. For now, the Interior Department keeps its discretion over federal leasing, and oil and gas companies are no worse off than before it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill has gone nowhere

industries.note: The bill guarantees the industry a steady stream of federal leases on public land and offshore waters on fixed terms, and bars any president from slowing leasing without congressional approval. The industry's gain comes from locking in access to publicly owned resources regardless of environmental review or market conditions; any benefit to consumers through energy supply is indirect and small relative to the access guaranteed to producers.

industries.industry: State economies in energy-producing states (WY, NM, MT, ND, CO, UT, OK, NV)
industries.note: Guaranteed annual onshore lease sales would bring drilling activity and federal mineral royalty revenue to these states, supporting local jobs and budgets.

industries.industry: Florida coastal tourism and Atlantic coastal communities
industries.note: The bill extends the eastern Gulf drilling ban through 2035 and expands it to the South Atlantic and Straits of Florida, protecting beaches and coastal economies from new offshore rigs.

analysis.trajectory: As a standalone bill, this is likely to stay in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee unless leadership decides it is worth floor time; most drilling-mandate bills at this stage die quietly. However, its core ideas — required lease sales and limits on a president's ability to pause leasing — have historically been attached to must-pass vehicles like budget reconciliation bills or broad permitting legislation, so elements of it could reappear in a larger energy package during this Congress.
